article.overview: A gas sampling instrument collects gas from the lunar surface, from regolith or from a spacecraft's exhaust plume, and passes it to an analyser that identifies the species present and their abundances. The Moon has only an extremely thin exosphere, so any gas to be measured must be captured efficiently, kept free of contamination from the spacecraft and the instrument itself, and then analysed. The payload name describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE) is the only flown lunar surface example in this article; it sampled ambient gas through an upward-facing aperture. Other examples are either unflown, or flew without reaching the Moon.
article.description: A sampling chain for lunar gas has three functional parts: an inlet that admits gas or gas-bearing material, a conditioning path that keeps the gas in a measurable state, and an analyser, commonly a mass spectrometer, that sorts the gas by mass. Sampling strategies differ. A surface instrument can sit in the exosphere and admit whatever gas reaches its aperture. A lander-mounted instrument can sample the exhaust plume of its own propulsion system as it descends. A regolith-oriented instrument must heat or otherwise extract volatiles from soil before the gas can be analysed. Each strategy has a distinct contamination risk: the lander or instrument may release its own gases, and the measured signal can be mistaken for lunar gas. For this reason, sampling design and analyser design cannot be separated in practice.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a gas sampling instrument is to determine what gases are present at or near the lunar surface, in what quantities, and how they change with time, lighting and location. Applications discussed in the sources include exosphere composition, lander exhaust interaction and regolith volatiles. LACE measured helium, neon and argon in the Apollo 17 exosphere and reported that its total density agreed with Cold Cathode Gauge measurements from earlier Apollo missions [1][2]. The NASA SEAL project aims to study how lunar regolith interacts with volatiles released from a lander's rocket exhaust, including whether water or CO2 stays in the soil or drifts into the exosphere, which bears on the stability of water at the poles [3]. Instruments such as the Bern Neutral Gas Mass Spectrometer (NGMS) were designed to investigate volatiles in lunar polar regolith as well as the exosphere, with a pyrolysis oven to release gas from soil samples [5][6].
article.operating_principle: Three operating principles recur in the sources. (1) Passive surface sampling: gas enters an aperture and is analysed in situ. LACE was a miniature magnetic-deflection mass spectrometer in which gas molecules were ionised by electron bombardment, formed into a beam, and passed through a magnetic analyser to a detector [4]. Its aperture faced upward to measure the downward flux of gas at the surface [1][2]. (2) Exhaust-plume sampling: SEAL is described as a spectrometer that measures gas released by the lander's propulsion system, beginning as the lander enters lunar orbit and continuing through descent, with sampling of molecules reaching the surface after touchdown [3]. (3) Heat-driven extraction from regolith: NGMS is described in the Bern project materials as part of a gas chromatography mass spectrometry package with a pyrolysis oven [6]. The 2025 IEEE paper title also indicates regolith and exosphere analysis [5]; the heating and transfer mechanism could not be verified from the readable text of that paper. In each case, the analyser's mass range, resolution and sensitivity determine which species can be identified, while the sampling design determines whether the measured gas is native to the Moon or derived from the spacecraft.
article.scientific_importance: Gas sampling is the main route to measuring the exosphere directly. Apollo-era instruments established that a tenuous atmosphere exists and that it contains helium, neon and argon. LACE's results have been interpreted as showing that most lunar helium originates from the solar wind, and that the argon-40 is consistent with radioactive decay of potassium-40 within the Moon [1][4]. These interpretations remain subject to the instrument's documented limitations. Modern instruments aim to distinguish lunar gas from lander outgassing, which the Peregrine experience has shown to be a serious issue.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a gas sampling instrument. The examples below were built for different missions, at different levels of maturity, and their available documentation varies widely. Values that could not be verified from the sources opened are reported as not stated rather than estimated.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE)
examples.status: Flown. Deployed by the Apollo 17 crew in Taurus-Littrow as part of the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP) on 12 December 1972.
examples.operating_dates: Turned on by ground command at 18:07 UTC on 27 December 1972. Sweep high voltage fell to zero on 17 October 1973 following a high-voltage fault.
examples.reported_detection_characteristics: Recording accuracy of 1 percent for 21-bit counts; detector saturation above 5 x 10^5 counts per second. Source: secondary (Wikipedia); not confirmed against the primary Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report.
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the NASA records or the secondary source checked. The normal sweep high-voltage figure (2900 V) is the only electrical value located.

examples.name: NASA Surface and Exosphere Alteration by Landers (SEAL)
examples.status: In development according to the NASA Goddard project page; no launch date stated. A NASA CLPS update dated 6 April 2023 (reported in a search result, not fetched) describes SEAL as reallocated to future lunar delivery missions.
examples.instrument_type: Spectrometer; mass spectrometer type not stated.
examples.origin: A search result states SEAL was built in 1998 as an engineering model for Japan's Nozomi spacecraft and later revived for a lunar commercial lander; not verified against the NASA page.
examples.qualification: Mass, power and dimensions are not stated. Target species conflict with a search summary listing N2, H2, NH3, H2O, CO and hydrocarbons; the NASA page was preferred.

examples.name: Bern Neutral Gas Mass Spectrometer (NGMS)
examples.type: Neutral gas mass spectrometer, developed for the Luna-25/Luna-27 programme (flight status not confirmed)
examples.status: Developed by the University of Bern. A search-result summary indicates NGMS was not aboard Luna-25 after descoping. The current status of NGMS hardware and any Luna-27 plans could not be confirmed from the Bern mission page, which gives only planned dates.
examples.instrument_type: Neutral gas mass spectrometer; regolith and exosphere analysis per the 2025 IEEE paper title. The time-of-flight, gas chromatography and pyrolysis configuration was not confirmed from a readable source.
examples.qualification: Mass, power, dimensions, mass range and detection limits are not stated in any source opened.

examples.name: Peregrine Ion Trap Mass Spectrometer (PITMS)
examples.type: Ion trap mass spectrometer operated as a passive sampler; flown but did not reach the Moon
examples.status: Flown on the Astrobotic Peregrine lander, which suffered a propulsion anomaly after launch and never reached the Moon. PITMS recorded 80 high-quality spectra in cislunar space.
examples.instrument_type: Ion trap mass spectrometer; gas enters through an aperture, is ionised and trapped in a radio-frequency field.
examples.scientific_outcome: Spectra were dominated by lander outgassing, including water and propulsion oxidiser; the authors conclude the spacecraft offgassed substantially more water than other planetary spacecraft. PITMS did not measure the native lunar exosphere.
examples.qualification: Performance values are from a search summary of Cohen et al. (2025), which was not fetched directly. Mass, dimensions and power not stated.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The four examples are not dimensionally comparable. LACE dimensions were not found in the sources opened. SEAL, NGMS and PITMS dimensions are not stated in the sources opened. A new gas sampling instrument would need its dimensions set by its inlet geometry, analyser type, thermal enclosure and mounting interface.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No verified mass is given for a generic gas sampling instrument. The LACE, SEAL, NGMS and PITMS masses are not stated in the sources opened. Mass matters for lander capacity and mounting design and must be verified for each instrument.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No verified power figure is given for a generic gas sampling instrument. The only LACE electrical value located is a normal sweep high-voltage output of 2900 V, which is not an input power figure.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A gas sampling instrument must operate in a near-vacuum with extreme temperature cycling and must avoid contaminating itself or its surroundings. The LACE record shows the consequences: sunrise raised background gas levels so much that operation was paused during the lunar day. The PITMS result shows that the lander's own outgassing can dominate measurements taken near the spacecraft. Good sampling therefore needs a clean inlet, a controlled thermal environment, and a plan to separate lunar gas from spacecraft gas. Instruments that heat regolith must also manage the risk of condensation in transfer lines. No verified figure for operating temperature, vacuum requirement or lifetime is given for a generic gas sampling instrument.
article.limitations: Contamination: lander exhaust and instrument outgassing can mimic or mask lunar gas, a major constraint for spacecraft-based measurements. Background variation: LACE data were strongly affected by local sunrise and by gas from the instrument's surroundings; suspected contaminants including H2, Cl2, O2, HCl and CO2 declined over time and rose with local sunrise and were considered probable instrument contaminants. Limited surface record: only one lunar surface gas sampling instrument has a reasonably documented flight record in this article, and its operation ended after about ten months. Unverified performance: most quantitative performance claims for recent instruments come from search summaries or titles rather than full papers read in this run.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface gas sampler must be integrated into a lander or surface package on Earth, launched, carried to the Moon, delivered to the surface, and oriented so that its inlet is in a defined position relative to the surface. Lander-mounted instruments such as SEAL depend on the lander's propulsion and on how the instrument is placed relative to the exhaust plume.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a lander or surface package on Earth, with inlet placement defined.
Launch it on a launch vehicle.
Deliver it to the surface on a lander, or carry it on a lander that descends with the instrument active.
Deploy and orient the inlet, then connect power, data and thermal interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For LACE, astronauts deployed the instrument as part of ALSEP with its aperture facing upward. SEAL was described as measuring from the lander as it enters orbit and descends, with post-touchdown sampling of exhaust molecules that reached the surface. Deployment method for NGMS and PITMS-class instruments is not verified.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LACE (Apollo 17, astronaut-deployed as part of ALSEP) is the only flown lunar surface example in this article. PITMS flew on Peregrine but did not reach the Moon.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. A specific gas sampling instrument would need its mass, dimensions, inlet location, data interface, power and thermal requirements compared with the target vehicle's verified specifications before any compatibility claim is made.

article.historical_significance: LACE flew on Apollo 17 as part of the ALSEP package and measured the lunar atmosphere from the surface. Its predecessors, the Cold Cathode Gauges on Apollo 14 and 15, had shown that a tenuous atmosphere existed but could not identify its composition. Later mass-spectrometer measurements from orbit, and the 2023 Peregrine attempt, are described only briefly in this article and were not reviewed in depth.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The instrument class is defined by function (sampling and analysing lunar gas) rather than by a single design; the examples are not interchangeable. LACE mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the NASA records checked. LACE detection figures come from a secondary source and need checking against the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report. SEAL target species conflict between sources, and its Nozomi origin and CLPS reallocation come from search summaries that need primary verification. The NGMS IEEE paper (2025) could not be read, so its time-of-flight, gas chromatography, pyrolysis and performance details are unverified. NGMS flight and Luna-27 status are not confirmed. PITMS performance values come from a search summary of Cohen et al. (2025). Commercial lunar gas-measurement payloads, including a NASA-funded regolith gas payload described in a news article, were not verified and are not included. No lunar site, lander or transportation compatibility is recommended, in line with the deferred location guidance.
